compare_runna_seo_title: OpenAthlete vs Runna: a free alternative for runners
compare_runna_seo_description: Runna gives you a ready-made plan. OpenAthlete gives you a free calendar, free plans, AI with your own key and room for a human coach.
compare_runna_intro_1: Runna is a very good app. You pick a race, it builds a plan written by coaches, adjusts it as you go, and sends each run to your watch. The phone experience is polished, and for a first half marathon it takes most of the guesswork away.
compare_runna_intro_2: It also costs {runnaYear} a year, has belonged to Strava since April 2025, and keeps its plan logic to itself. OpenAthlete works the other way round: a free calendar you or your coach control, free plans to start from, and AI that writes sessions when you ask.
compare_runna_summary_them: You want a plan that adjusts itself in a polished phone app, without thinking about it.
compare_runna_summary_oa: You want to own your plan, maybe with a coach, see your load, and not pay a subscription for it.
compare_runna_row_plans: Adaptive plans from 5K to marathon, written by coaches
compare_runna_oa_workout_sync: Garmin, Suunto, COROS. No Apple Watch.
compare_runna_better_oa_1_body: Calendar, workout builder, watch sync, analysis and training load cost nothing. Runna is {runnaYear} a year, or {bundle} with Strava.
compare_runna_better_oa_2_body: Invite a coach. They see every session, your answers to the post-run questions, and any pain you report.
compare_runna_better_oa_3_body: Fitness, fatigue and form, projected over the weeks ahead. You see a block ramping too fast instead of taking the app's word for it.
compare_runna_better_oa_4_body: Trail, cycling, swimming, triathlon and 50+ sport types on one calendar.
compare_runna_better_them_1_body: Runna reworks your plan as the weeks go by. OpenAthlete has no automatic plan generator: you, your coach, or an AI assistant through MCP adjust the calendar.
compare_runna_better_them_2_body: Runna is built for the phone, and it shows. Our Android app is on Google Play and our iPhone app is in testing; on iPhone, OpenAthlete is an installable web app for now.
compare_runna_better_them_3_body: Runna sends runs to Apple Watch. OpenAthlete doesn't.
compare_runna_switch_note: Mid-plan? Finish the block on Runna, then start fresh: pick a free plan on this site for your distance and goal time, and import it into your calendar.
compare_runna_faq_1_q: Is there a free alternative to Runna?
compare_runna_faq_1_a: OpenAthlete is free: calendar, structured workouts sent to Garmin, Suunto and COROS, training load and analysis. Free running, trail and triathlon plans on this site import straight into it.
compare_runna_faq_2_q: Does OpenAthlete build adaptive plans like Runna?
compare_runna_faq_2_a: No. The AI writes or edits single sessions from a sentence, and an assistant like Claude or ChatGPT can plan a whole block through the MCP server. Nothing reshapes your plan behind your back: you or your coach decide.
compare_runna_faq_3_q: Does it work with my Apple Watch?
compare_runna_faq_3_a: Not directly. OpenAthlete connects to Garmin, COROS, Suunto, Polar and Strava, and reads FIT, GPX and TCX files. If your Apple Watch runs reach Strava, they can come in from there.
compare_runna_faq_4_a: Yes. Connect it and OpenAthlete imports every activity, plus your full history on request. Nothing is posted back to Strava.
compare_strava_seo_title: OpenAthlete vs Strava: open-source alternative from Europe
compare_strava_seo_description: Strava is for sharing; OpenAthlete is for training. Plans, structured workouts, training load and full data ownership. Keep Strava synced if you like.
compare_strava_intro_1: Strava is where your running club lives. Kudos, segments, routes, the photos from Sunday's ride: nobody does the social side better, and we're not trying to.
compare_strava_intro_2: OpenAthlete does the other half: planning the next block, sending structured workouts to the watch, tracking fitness and fatigue, working with a coach. You can use both. Connect Strava and every activity comes in, history included.
compare_strava_summary_them: You want the feed, kudos, segments and routes. Keep it.
compare_strava_summary_oa: You want to plan, send workouts to the watch and follow your load, for free.
compare_strava_row_purpose: Sharing: feed, kudos, clubs, segments, routes
compare_strava_row_social: Its core: feed, kudos, clubs, segments
compare_strava_row_plans: Through Runna, sold separately or {bundle}/year in a bundle
compare_strava_better_oa_1_body: Plan sessions, races and blocks, drag templates in, copy a week, and see done against planned at a glance.
compare_strava_better_oa_2_body: Structured sessions like 5 × 4' at threshold go to Garmin, Suunto and COROS watches, with your zones.
compare_strava_better_oa_3_body: Fitness, fatigue and form from heart rate or RPE, projected over what you've planned. The formulas are public.
compare_strava_better_oa_4_body: No public feed, no ads. Open source code, servers in France, full JSON export and complete account deletion.
compare_strava_better_them_1_body: Feed, kudos, clubs and comments from friends. OpenAthlete has messaging with your coach, not a social feed.
compare_strava_better_them_2_body: Segment leaderboards and route building. We have neither.
compare_strava_better_them_3_body: Mature iOS and Android apps. Ours is on Google Play for Android and in testing for iPhone; there, OpenAthlete is an installable web app for now.
compare_strava_switch_note: There's nothing to leave. Connect Strava in Settings > Connectors, press Import all activities, and keep posting to Strava as usual. Connect your watch brand directly too if you want planned workouts on it.
compare_strava_faq_1_a: For training, yes: planning, structured workouts, training load and coaching. For the social side, no. You can keep Strava for that and connect it.
compare_strava_faq_2_a: No. It imports from Strava (every new activity, plus your full history on request) and sends nothing back.
compare_strava_faq_3_q: Should I connect Strava or my watch?
compare_strava_faq_3_a: Both, ideally. Strava brings your history in quickly. Your watch account (Garmin, Suunto, COROS) is what receives planned workouts, and Garmin, Polar, Suunto and COROS also share wellness data like sleep and HRV.
compare_strava_faq_4_a: Yes, every feature, on our servers or yours. Supporter ({oaMonth}/month or {oaYear}/year) adds AI on our keys and unlimited coached athletes. Strava's subscription is {stravaYear} a year.
features_tl_seo_title: Training load: fitness, fatigue and form (CTL, ATL, TSB)
features_tl_seo_description: See fitness, fatigue and form from every session, with or without a power meter. TRIMP-based load, transparent formulas, open-source code.
features_tl_title: Know when to push and when to rest
features_tl_lead: Every session with a heart rate becomes a load. From those loads come three curves: fitness, fatigue and form. They run into the weeks you have planned, so you see race-day form before race day.
features_tl_curves_title: What CTL, ATL and TSB mean
features_tl_curves_lead: The Banister model, the same idea behind most training-load charts. Two averages of your daily load, one slow and one fast, and the gap between them.
features_tl_ctl_body: What months of training have built. It moves slowly: a great week barely nudges it, a month off pulls it down.
features_tl_atl_body: What the last week costs you. It rises fast after hard days and falls fast when you rest.
features_tl_tsb_body: Fitness minus fatigue. Negative while you are loading, back above zero when you ease off before a race.
features_tl_formula_note: One day weighs 1 − e^(−1/τ), the exact decay of the model. The common 2 / (N + 1) shortcut would quietly halve both time constants, so we don't use it. Rest days count as zero and make both curves fall.
features_tl_trimp_body: Banister's training impulse multiplies time by how far into your heart rate reserve you were, and weights the hard minutes exponentially. One hour easy and twenty minutes hard can cost the same. The app integrates your heart rate second by second; with only an average it uses that.
features_tl_trimp_needs: It needs your maximum and resting heart rate in your metrics. Without a heart rate, an activity adds no TRIMP.
features_tl_trimp_coeffs: Coefficients: 0.64 and 1.92 for men, 0.86 and 1.67 for women.
features_tl_rpe_body: Give an activity an effort score from 0 to 10 and the app also computes Foster's session RPE: RPE × minutes. 50 minutes at RPE 6 makes 300. Useful to compare how hard it felt with what your heart said. The fitness curve itself stays on TRIMP, so the two scales never mix.
features_tl_plan_title: See race-day form before race day
features_tl_plan_body: Planned sessions get an estimated load in the same TRIMP unit, so done and planned add up. Fitness, fatigue and form then continue over the plan, day by day on the calendar and week by week on the season view. Move a long run and the curve moves with it.
features_tl_plan_method_title: How a planned session gets its load
features_tl_plan_method_1: Heart rate targets: summed step by step, because the formula is not linear.
features_tl_plan_method_2: Pace or power targets: an AI estimate calibrated on your past sessions, if AI is set up.
features_tl_plan_method_3: Otherwise: planned duration and target RPE, converted to the heart rate that effort usually brings. No AI key needed.
features_tl_weekly: Each week also shows its load against a recommended range built from your recent weeks. It is a rule of thumb to frame a week, not a safety limit.
features_tl_read_title: Reading your form before a race
features_tl_read_body: During a training block, form usually sits below zero: you are carrying fatigue on purpose. In the taper, fatigue drops faster than fitness and form climbs back above zero. Most people aim to arrive at a race slightly positive, not as high as possible: too long a taper costs fitness.
features_tl_gauge_note: The two marks, −20 and +25, are the ones in OpenAthlete's code. They are conventions to describe the curve, not validated limits: −25 is not a diagnosis of overreaching, and a taper reaches +25 too.
features_tl_diff_title: Why our numbers differ from your watch
features_tl_diff_body: Garmin, COROS, Suunto and Polar each compute their own training load with their own models, mostly closed. TrainingPeaks uses TSS, where one hour at threshold is 100. OpenAthlete uses Banister TRIMP from heart rate. The scales are different, so a TRIMP of 108 is not "more" than a TSS of 80. Compare the trend of one system with itself.
features_tl_open_title: Formulas you can audit on GitHub
features_tl_open_body: No black box. The constants, their sources and the code that turns a heart rate stream into fitness are public, under AGPL-3.0. Found a mistake? Open an issue. In the app, every derived metric has a short "what it is" and "limits" note.
features_tl_open_file_1: TRIMP, planned load and the daily CTL/ATL step
features_tl_open_file_2: Coefficients, time constants and form thresholds, with references
features_tl_open_file_3: The science behind each statistic, in the docs
features_tl_faq_1_q: Do I need a power meter?
features_tl_faq_1_a: No. Load comes from heart rate, from a chest strap or the watch's wrist sensor. You need your maximum and resting heart rate in your metrics.
features_tl_faq_2_q: What about a swim or a session without heart rate?
features_tl_faq_2_a: It adds no TRIMP, so it does not move the fitness curve. If you give it an RPE, its session RPE (RPE × minutes) is still computed and shown.
features_tl_faq_3_q: Why is my fitness lower than on TrainingPeaks or Garmin?
features_tl_faq_3_a: Different unit. TRIMP and TSS are different scales, and watch brands use their own models. Look at the shape of the curve over weeks, not at the number.
features_tl_faq_4_a: No. Sessions with heart rate targets, or with a duration and a target RPE, are estimated by formula. AI only helps for sessions written in pace or power.
features_tl_faq_5_q: Can my coach see my form?
features_tl_faq_5_a: Yes. The coach dashboard shows fitness, fatigue and form for each athlete next to compliance and volume.
features_tl_final_title: See where your form is heading
features_tl_final_body: Connect your watch: your activities come in, the curves draw themselves, and the next three weeks of your plan show up as dashed lines.
features_ai_seo_title: AI running and triathlon coach, with your own AI key
features_ai_seo_description: AI from your real training: sessions from a sentence, questions after each run, a read of every activity. OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, with your own key.
features_ai_title: An AI coach that knows your training
features_ai_lead: Not a chatbot glued onto a calendar. A few precise jobs, done with your zones, your activities and your own words: write a session from a sentence, ask how the run went, read what happened. On your own AI key, or on ours with Supporter.
features_ai_read_headline: Threshold held for four reps, the fifth faded
features_ai_read_f1: 4 of 5 reps on target (4:05–4:12 /km). Rep 5 at 4:17.
features_ai_read_f2: 24 °C and a headwind on the way back cost about 6 s/km.
features_ai_read_f3: You wrote "legs heavy from Sunday": your fatigue is the highest in five weeks.
features_ai_q: How did your legs feel on the last rep?
features_ai_q_noted: Noted by the AI · RPE 8 · left calf, pain 3/10
features_ai_jobs_title: Grounded in your data, not generic plans
features_ai_jobs_lead: Each AI feature has one job and the data it needs for it. Nothing runs before you allow it.
features_ai_job_1_body: "10' easy, 6 × 3' at 95% VMA with 2' jog." You get a structured workout with steps, repeats and targets from your zones and latest metrics. Edit it like any other, then it goes to your watch.
features_ai_job_2_body: "Make it 20 minutes shorter", "swap the hills for flat tempo". The session is rewritten; you check it before saving.
features_ai_job_3_body: Three or four short questions about feeling, fatigue, sleep, pain or why you left the plan, adapted to your load and past injuries. Answer by text, a tap or your voice. Effort (RPE) and pain are pulled out and land in an injury log your coach sees.
features_ai_job_4_body: A headline, up to three findings with figures (plan vs done, what the heat cost, drift, last weeks), one suggestion. On the activity page, where you look anyway.
features_ai_job_5_body: For sessions written in pace or power, an estimate of the load calibrated on your past sessions, so the form projection covers them too.
features_ai_byok_title: Choose the model, control the cost
features_ai_byok_body: Paste an API key from the provider you already use. Pick a default model, then a different one per feature if you like: a cheap fast model for the questions, a stronger one to write sessions. You pay the provider directly, and a meter shows tokens and calls per month, per feature.
features_ai_byok_local: Self-hosted instances can also point at an OpenAI-compatible endpoint: Ollama, vLLM, a model on your own machine.
features_ai_pay_title: Your key first, then the Supporter allowance
features_ai_pay_body: When an AI feature runs, OpenAthlete looks for something to pay for it, in this order. If it finds nothing, the AI stays off and the rest of the app works exactly the same.
features_ai_pay_1_body: Any plan, Free included. The model you chose for that feature.
features_ai_pay_2_body: €5 a month or €50 a year: AI on OpenAthlete's keys, up to a monthly allowance. Past it, add your own key.
features_ai_pay_3_body: For the questions and reads after your activities, your coach's key or Supporter allowance can cover you, with both your consents.
features_ai_pay_4_body: AI off. Calendar, builder, sync, analysis and coaching all work.
features_ai_pay_selfhost: On a self-hosted instance, the admin decides who may use the instance's keys: everyone, nobody, or Supporters if billing is set up.
features_ai_coach_body: The AI drafts, you decide. Generated sessions are drafts you edit before they reach the athlete. You can switch off the post-activity questions for any athlete. Pain reported in answers shows up in your dashboard's "to watch" list.
features_ai_coach_point_1: One Supporter coach can power the background AI of all their athletes
features_ai_coach_point_2: Athletes can turn the questions off too
features_ai_mcp_title: Want to talk it through? Use Claude or ChatGPT
features_ai_mcp_body: There is no chat window inside OpenAthlete. Conversations, and planning a whole block, happen in the assistant you already use, connected to your training through our MCP server. It reads your calendar and load, and can plan up to 60 sessions at once.
features_ai_mcp_prompt: Work trip Wednesday to Friday, hotel treadmill only. Can you fix my week?
features_ai_mcp_reply: Done. Thursday's long intervals move to Monday, Wednesday becomes 40' easy on the treadmill, and Friday is now rest. Your form on Sunday stays at +4.
features_ai_privacy_1_body: No AI runs on your data until you allow it in your settings, after an explanation of what goes where. You can withdraw it at any time.
features_ai_privacy_2_body: Your zones, recent metrics, the activity and your answers go to the provider of the model that runs the task. Your password, email and payment details do not.
features_ai_privacy_3_body: API keys are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and never shown again after you save them. Delete one and it is gone.
features_ai_limit_1: No chat inside the app. Conversation goes through Claude, ChatGPT or another assistant over MCP.
features_ai_limit_2: No one-click full training plan in the app. Plan blocks with an assistant over MCP, or with your coach.
features_ai_limit_3: No weekly AI report, no fatigue or injury-risk prediction.
features_ai_limit_4: Voice answers are turned into text. Tone and mood are not analysed.
features_ai_limit_5: It is not a doctor. Pain in the injury log is a flag for you and your coach, not a diagnosis.
features_ai_faq_1_q: Do I have to pay to use the AI?
features_ai_faq_1_a: Not OpenAthlete. With your own key, on any plan, you pay your AI provider for what you use. Supporter (€5 a month) includes a monthly allowance on our keys instead. Without either, the AI features stay off and everything else works.
features_ai_faq_2_a: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, xAI, Groq, OVHcloud, Scaleway, Together AI, Fireworks and many more from the models.dev catalogue. You pick the model per feature.
features_ai_faq_3_q: Can I use a local model?
features_ai_faq_3_a: On a self-hosted instance, yes: point it at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as Ollama or vLLM. On OpenAthlete Cloud, custom endpoints are turned off.
features_ai_faq_4_q: Is there an AI chat in the app?
features_ai_faq_4_a: No. The chat bubble in the app is for messages between athletes and coaches. To talk with an AI about your training, connect Claude, ChatGPT or another assistant to the MCP server.
features_ai_faq_5_q: How big is the Supporter allowance?
features_ai_faq_5_a: It is a monthly budget per person, measured at the provider's prices. The usage meter in your settings shows where you are. When it runs out, add your own key or wait for next month.
features_ai_faq_6_a: Yes. Withdraw AI consent and nothing runs on your data. You can also turn off only the post-activity questions, and so can your coach.
features_ai_final_title: Try it on your next run
features_ai_final_body: Create an account, add your key or become a Supporter, and the questions show up after your next synced activity.
plans_hub_seo_title: Free training plans: 10K, half marathon, marathon, trail
plans_hub_seo_description: Free week-by-week plans for 10K, half marathon, marathon and trail, with pace targets from your VMA. Import one into OpenAthlete and send it to your watch.
plans_hub_h1: Free training plans, every session written out
plans_hub_lead: Read the whole plan here, week by week. If you like it, import it into OpenAthlete in one click: it lands in your calendar from the start date you choose, and the structured sessions go to your Garmin, Suunto or COROS.
plans_hub_running_body: 10K from 40 min to 1h00, half marathon from 1h30 to 2h00, marathon from 3h00 to 5h30. Every session has its target.
plans_hub_trail_body: Plans for 20 km, 30 km and 50 km by elevation gain, with hill repeats, power hiking and downhill work.
plans_hub_triathlon_body: Sprint, Olympic and 70.3, with swim, bike and run in one calendar. Being written.

plans_hub_how_1: Pick a plan and read it through. Nothing to sign up for.
plans_hub_how_2: Click import, create a free account, choose your start date.
plans_hub_how_3: Move sessions around your week; structured ones reach your Garmin, Suunto or COROS.
plans_hub_final_title: A plan is a draft. Your calendar is the real thing.
plans_hub_final_body: Import a plan, then move, shorten or swap sessions as your weeks happen. Fitness and fatigue follow.
plans_hub_soon_body: We would rather publish a few plans that hold up than a hundred generated ones. Until they are out, you can build your own sessions in OpenAthlete, or ask Claude or ChatGPT to plan a block through the MCP server and get it straight into your calendar.
plans_hub_running_seo_title: Free running plans: 10K, half marathon and marathon
plans_hub_running_seo_description: Free plans for the 10K (40 min–1h00), half (1h30–2h00) and marathon (3h00–5h30). 3 to 5 runs a week, targets in % of VMA and goal pace, sent to your watch.

plans_hub_trail_seo_description: Free trail plans for 20 km/800 m D+, 30 km/1,000 m D+ and 50 km/2,500 m D+. Every session written out, with targets set to your paces and heart rate.

plans_hub_triathlon_seo_description: Triathlon plans for sprint, Olympic and 70.3 are being written. Meanwhile, plan swim, bike and run sessions in one calendar with OpenAthlete.
tplan_seo_description: Free {weeks}-week {distance} plan to finish in {time}, with targets from your VMA. Import it into OpenAthlete and send it to Garmin, COROS or Suunto.
tplan_import_note: Free account, you choose the start date. Every session can be moved or edited afterwards.
tplan_schedule_lead: Every session with its targets. Each one carries a step-by-step workout that goes to your watch once the plan is imported.
tplan_paces_body: Finishing in {time} means {pace} per kilometre on average. The plan writes every target as a share of VMA or as this goal pace. If your recent races say otherwise, check your VMA or a recent result before you start.
tplan_fallback: This plan is not translated into your language yet: the sessions below are in English.
tplan_watch_title: Send the plan to your watch
tplan_watch_body: Once imported, structured sessions go to Garmin, Suunto and COROS watches with their steps and paces. Activities come back from your watch or Strava and are matched to the planned session.
features_mcp_seo_title: Training MCP server for Claude and ChatGPT | OpenAthlete
features_mcp_seo_description: Connect Claude, ChatGPT or any MCP client to your training: read load and activities, plan sessions that sync to your watch. Free, open source.
features_mcp_title: Your training, inside Claude and ChatGPT
features_mcp_lead: Connect the assistant you already pay for to OpenAthlete. It reads your calendar, activities and form, and with your permission plans a 12-week block straight into your calendar. From there, the sessions go to your watch.
features_mcp_chat_prompt: Build me a 12-week plan for a marathon on 14 March, 5 runs a week, long run on Sundays.
features_mcp_chat_reply: Your plan is in the calendar: 60 sessions in 4 blocks, threshold on Tuesdays, long runs from 1h30 to 2h50 on Sundays, a lighter week every fourth, two weeks of taper. Workouts will reach your Garmin as their dates come up.
features_mcp_what_body: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard that lets an AI assistant use tools provided by another app. OpenAthlete is an MCP server: once connected, Claude or ChatGPT can call functions like get_training_load or plan_sessions on your account, the way you would click through the app. The model runs on your assistant's side, so OpenAthlete pays nothing for it, and neither do you: the MCP server is free on every plan, self-hosted instances included.
features_mcp_ask_lead: Four requests and the tools the assistant calls to answer them.
features_mcp_ask_1: Build me a 12-week plan for a marathon on 14 March, 5 runs a week, with my long run on Sundays.
features_mcp_ask_2: I've had a fever since yesterday. Adapt my next two weeks.
features_mcp_ask_3: How did last week go compared to the plan? Is my form right for Saturday's race?
features_mcp_ask_4: My new FTP is 265 W: record it and update my power zones.
features_mcp_tools_lead: Workouts read and write in plain units: durations in seconds, paces as 4:35 per km, your zones by id, or percentages of VMA, FTP or maximum heart rate. Dates are in your time zone.
features_mcp_t_context: Today's date and time zone, metrics, zones, fitness and form, the last 4 weeks, coming races, periods and injuries. Agents call it first.
features_mcp_t_calendar: Planned sessions (done, missed or to do), races, notes, activities and periods between two dates.
features_mcp_t_session: A session's structured workout; an activity's laps and your answers to the post-activity questions.
features_mcp_t_history: Training history and weekly volume per sport.
features_mcp_t_load: Weekly load, done and planned, with fitness, fatigue and form projected over the planned sessions.
features_mcp_t_metrics: Metric history (weight, resting HR, HRV, sleep), capacities and best efforts.
features_mcp_t_library: Your workout library; for coaches, the athletes they coach.
features_mcp_t_plan: Adds up to 60 trainings with structured workouts, races and notes at once. All are saved, or none.
features_mcp_t_update: Changes a session, a race or a note; for a repeated session, this one and the following.
features_mcp_t_move: Moves or copies sessions by days, repeats one every few weeks.
features_mcp_t_delete: Deletes planned sessions. Done sessions and recorded activities are never deleted.
features_mcp_t_period: Training blocks, and periods without training: travel, illness, injury.
features_mcp_t_log: Records measurements, changes a zone after a test.
features_mcp_setup_lead: The address is the same everywhere. On a self-hosted instance it is https://<your domain>/api/mcp.
features_mcp_setup_claude_sub: claude.ai and desktop app, then on mobile too. One custom connector on the free plan
features_mcp_setup_claude_3: Sign in to OpenAthlete and choose Allow
features_mcp_setup_chatgpt_sub: Business, Enterprise and Edu plans when we checked; Pro can only read
features_mcp_setup_chatgpt_2: Paste the address, choose OAuth, create it as a plugin
features_mcp_setup_code_sub: In a terminal, then /mcp to sign in
features_mcp_setup_other_title: Cursor, VS Code, your own agent
features_mcp_setup_other_sub: OAuth if the client supports it, otherwise a personal token from Settings › AI agents, shown once
features_mcp_coach_body: A coach's assistant reaches the athletes they coach, with the same rules as in the app. It lists them, then passes the athlete with each request. Ask for a review of everyone's week, or rework one athlete's block after a bad cold.
features_mcp_coach_prompt: For each of my athletes, how did last week compare to the plan?
features_mcp_coach_reply: Four of six hit 90% or more of planned time. Léa missed both quality sessions and wrote "calf tight" on Thursday. Marc did 30% more than planned.
features_mcp_sec_1: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE: you approve each assistant on an OpenAthlete page. It never sees your password.
features_mcp_sec_2: Read and write are separate. An assistant with read access is not even offered the tools that write.
features_mcp_sec_3: Tokens are stored hashed. Access tokens last an hour; refresh tokens are single-use, and a stolen one used twice revokes the access.
features_mcp_sec_4: Personal tokens last 30, 90 or 365 days, or never expire. Revoke any connection in Settings › AI agents; it stops at the next request.
features_mcp_sec_5: Assistants reach your training, not your account: no password change, no device or subscription change, no deleting your history.
features_mcp_sec_note: What an assistant does with your data is up to it and its provider. Connect the ones you trust.

features_mcp_faq_2_a: Claude (claude.ai, desktop, mobile and Claude Code), ChatGPT in developer mode, Cursor, VS Code and any MCP client that supports OAuth or a bearer token.

tools_hr_how_example: Example: resting 50 bpm, max 190 bpm, so a reserve of 140 beats. Zone 2 (60 to 70%) runs from 50 + 0.6 × 140 = 134 bpm to 50 + 0.7 × 140 = 148 bpm. With the percentage of max, the same zone would be 114 to 133 bpm.
tools_hr_how_max: Formulas that estimate max heart rate from age are off by 10 beats or more for many people. A max seen at the end of a hard race or a hill session is worth more.
tools_hr_faq4_q: What is my zone 2 heart rate?
tools_hr_faq4_a: With Karvonen, zone 2 is resting HR + 60 to 70% of your heart rate reserve. Enter your resting and max heart rate in the calculator above: zone 2 is shown in bpm. It is the pace of long runs and most easy days, where you can still talk in full sentences.
tools_hr_faq5_a: Target heart rate = resting HR + (max HR − resting HR) × intensity. Finnish physiologist Martti Karvonen proposed it in 1957 to set training intensity from the heart rate reserve rather than from max heart rate alone.
tools_rp_how_example: Example: a 10K in 45:00 predicts 21:35 for 5K, 1:39:17 for the half marathon (45:00 × 2.10975^1.06) and 3:27:01 for the marathon (45:00 × 4.2195^1.06).
tools_rp_how_source: Source: Peter Riegel, an American research engineer and marathoner, first published it in Runner's World in 1977, then in "Athletic Records and Human Endurance", American Scientist, vol. 69, 1981, from world records between roughly 3.5 minutes and 4 hours.
tools_rp_faq4_q: Where does the 1.06 exponent come from?
tools_rp_faq4_a: Riegel fitted it to world records in running. An exponent of 1 would mean holding the same pace whatever the distance; 1.06 is the slowdown records show. Some coaches use 1.07 or 1.08 for recreational runners over the marathon, which gives slower, often more realistic predictions.

aig_claude_faq_1_q: Do I need a paid Claude plan?
aig_claude_faq_1_a: No. On 3 November 2026, Anthropic's help centre lists custom connectors on the free plan, limited to one connector. Paid plans allow more than one.
aig_claude_faq_2_a: No. The connector and its 23 tools work on a free account. Supporter only adds AI inside OpenAthlete on our keys and unlimited coached athletes.
aig_claude_faq_3_q: Will the sessions Claude plans reach my watch?
aig_claude_faq_3_a: On Garmin, COROS and Suunto, yes: they go out like the sessions you plan yourself in OpenAthlete. Polar only sends activities in.
aig_claude_faq_4_a: No. With write access it can move, change or delete planned sessions, but done sessions and recorded activities are out of reach. Anything it planned can be edited in your calendar.
aig_claude_faq_5_q: Does it work on my phone?
aig_claude_faq_5_a: Yes. Add the connector on claude.ai or in Claude Desktop; Anthropic says it is then available in the Claude iOS and Android apps.
aig_claude_faq_6_q: Can my coach use it too?
aig_claude_faq_6_a: Yes. A coach who connects Claude reaches the athletes they coach in OpenAthlete, with the same rights as in the app. Up to 5 athletes on the free plan, unlimited with Supporter.
aig_claude_faq_7_q: Claude or ChatGPT: which one should I use?
aig_claude_faq_7_a: The connector is the same. What differs is the plan you need: on 3 November 2026, Claude allowed one custom connector with read and write on its free plan, while ChatGPT kept write actions for Business, Enterprise and Edu.
aig_chatgpt_faq_1_q: Which ChatGPT plan do I need?
aig_chatgpt_faq_1_a: On 3 November 2026, OpenAI offered full custom MCP servers, write actions included, on Business, Enterprise and Edu (in beta, on the web). Pro could connect them read-only. Free and Plus could not. These rules change often: your Plugins page has the final word.
aig_chatgpt_faq_2_a: No. The MCP server and its 23 tools work on a free account. Supporter only adds AI inside OpenAthlete on our keys and unlimited coached athletes.
aig_chatgpt_faq_3_q: Why does ChatGPT ask me to confirm every change?
aig_chatgpt_faq_3_a: OpenAthlete marks its read tools as read-only, so ChatGPT treats everything else (planning, moving, deleting) as a write action and asks first. You can remember your choice for a tool until the end of the conversation.
aig_chatgpt_faq_4_a: No. With write access it can move, change or delete planned sessions, but done sessions and recorded activities are out of reach. Anything it planned can be edited in your calendar.
aig_chatgpt_faq_5_q: Will the sessions ChatGPT plans reach my watch?
aig_chatgpt_faq_5_a: On Garmin, COROS and Suunto, yes, provided your ChatGPT plan allows write actions. Polar only sends activities in.
aig_chatgpt_faq_6_q: Does it work in the ChatGPT phone app?
aig_chatgpt_faq_6_a: OpenAI documents the setup and custom MCP servers on the web, and we have not been able to confirm mobile support. Set it up on chatgpt.com in a browser.
aig_chatgpt_faq_7_q: My plan doesn't allow custom MCP servers. What now?
aig_chatgpt_faq_7_a: Use the same connector from another client. Claude's free plan allows one custom connector with read and write, and Cursor, VS Code or your own agent work with a personal token from Settings › AI agents.

aib_garmin_seo_title: Garmin + Claude/ChatGPT: your Garmin data in AI, via MCP
aib_garmin_seo_description: Connect Garmin to Claude or ChatGPT through OpenAthlete's MCP server: ask about activities, sleep and HRV, plan workouts that land on your watch. Free.
aib_garmin_h1: Talk to Claude or ChatGPT about your Garmin training
aib_garmin_lead: Garmin doesn't publish an MCP server. OpenAthlete is one: it syncs your activities, sleep and HRV through Garmin's official API, lets Claude or ChatGPT read them, and sends the structured workouts the assistant plans to your watch.
aib_garmin_chat_prompt: Compare my HRV this week with last month and tell me whether to keep Thursday's threshold session.
aib_garmin_chat_reply: Your overnight HRV averaged 48 ms this week against 56 ms over the last 30 days, and resting HR is up 4 bpm. I'd swap Thursday's 3 × 10' at threshold for 45' easy and move it to Saturday. Shall I make the change? It will sync to your Forerunner.
aib_garmin_auth_contrast: Community Garmin MCP servers such as mcp-garmin sign in to Garmin Connect with your email and password, through an unofficial library, and keep the session on your computer. OpenAthlete uses Garmin's official partner API: you sign in on Garmin's page and OpenAthlete only receives a token you can revoke.
aib_garmin_activities: Every new activity, with laps and the full recording
aib_garmin_metrics: Sleep stages and score, overnight HRV, resting HR, stress, Body Battery, VO2max, SpO2, respiration, steps, body composition
aib_garmin_watch: Yes: to the Garmin Connect calendar, then the watch at its next sync. Running, cycling, pool swimming, strength and more
aib_garmin_p1: My Body Battery hasn't gone above 60 all week. Look at my sleep and load and lighten the next four days.
aib_garmin_p2: Build me 10 weeks to a sub-1:45 half marathon, four runs a week, long run on Sunday, and send it to my Forerunner.
aib_garmin_p3: How much does my heart rate drift on runs longer than two hours, compared with last spring?
aib_garmin_p4: Work trip Monday to Wednesday, hotel treadmill only. Rework the week.
aib_garmin_p5: My lactate threshold test gave 171 bpm. Update my zones and tell me which sessions change.
aib_garmin_own_1: No MCP server published by Garmin.
aib_garmin_own_2: Garmin Connect+ ($6.99 a month in the US at launch) adds Active Intelligence: AI insights and suggestions in the Garmin Connect app, in beta.
aib_garmin_own_3: Community MCP servers exist; the ones we checked sign in with your Garmin Connect email and password.
aib_garmin_oa_write: Plans structured sessions in your calendar; they reach Garmin Connect and your watch.
aib_garmin_vs_note: Connect+ and OpenAthlete do not exclude each other: Active Intelligence stays in the Garmin app, OpenAthlete opens your data to the assistant you choose.
aib_garmin_faq_1_q: Is there an official Garmin MCP server?
aib_garmin_faq_1_a: Not that we could find on 3 November 2026. Garmin's AI features live in Garmin Connect+ (Active Intelligence, in beta). The Garmin MCP servers on GitHub are community projects, and the ones we checked sign in with your Garmin Connect email and password. OpenAthlete connects through Garmin's official API instead.
aib_garmin_faq_2_q: Can Claude send a workout to my Garmin watch?
aib_garmin_faq_2_a: Yes, through OpenAthlete. The assistant plans the session in your OpenAthlete calendar with plan_sessions. With workout export on, OpenAthlete pushes it to the Garmin Connect calendar and your watch picks it up at its next sync.
aib_garmin_faq_3_q: Can ChatGPT read my Garmin sleep and HRV?
aib_garmin_faq_3_a: Yes, once you turn on metric import for Garmin in OpenAthlete (it is off by default). Sleep, overnight HRV, resting heart rate, stress and Body Battery then come in every day, and the assistant reads them with get_metrics.
aib_garmin_faq_4_q: How much of my Garmin history does the AI see?
aib_garmin_faq_4_a: Garmin lets OpenAthlete import the last 30 days when you connect, then every new activity. To go further back, export your data from Garmin and drop the FIT files on the OpenAthlete calendar.
aib_coros_seo_title: COROS + Claude/ChatGPT: your COROS data in AI, via MCP
aib_coros_seo_description: Use Claude or ChatGPT with your COROS watch through OpenAthlete's MCP server: activities, HRV, sleep, load, and workouts sent to the watch. Free.
aib_coros_h1: Claude and ChatGPT, with your COROS training behind them
aib_coros_lead: COROS has its own MCP server, and OpenAthlete uses it to sync your watch. On top, OpenAthlete adds a calendar with training load, your other devices and your coach, and lets Claude or ChatGPT plan run, trail and bike workouts that go to your COROS.
aib_coros_chat_prompt: Trail race in eight weeks: 50 km, 2,400 m of climbing. Check my weekly vertical and plan the next four weeks.
aib_coros_chat_reply: Since September you've averaged 1,150 m of climbing a week, with one 1,900 m week. You climb 1,000 m/h on 15–20% slopes. I've planned four weeks building to 2,000 m: hill repeats on Tuesdays (8 × 3' uphill at threshold), a long hilly run on Saturdays, the fourth week lighter. 16 sessions, heading to your APEX 2 Pro.
aib_coros_auth_contrast: COROS's own MCP server uses OAuth too, and OpenAthlete connects through it: you sign in on COROS's page, pick your region, and OpenAthlete receives a token.
aib_coros_activities: Every new activity, fetched about every 30 minutes (COROS sends no notifications)
aib_coros_history: All of it, at COROS's pace: 50 activity files a day, so years of training take several days
aib_coros_metrics: HRV, resting heart rate, sleep, naps, VO2max
aib_coros_watch: Yes, for running, trail running and cycling. COROS does not let apps delete a planned session: a deleted one becomes a “removed” placeholder
aib_coros_p1: What is my climbing speed on 15 to 20% slopes? Use it to estimate my time on a 900 m climb.
aib_coros_p2: My HRV has been low three nights running. Should I still do Saturday's long run?
aib_coros_p3: Copy last week to next week, but turn the Wednesday intervals into hill repeats.
aib_coros_p4: I rolled my ankle on a descent today. Log it and rework the next ten days.
aib_coros_p5: How does my heart rate drift on outings over four hours? I want to pace the first half of my 50 km.
aib_coros_own_1: An official MCP server (mcp.coros.com/mcp) since May 2026, for Claude, ChatGPT in developer mode, Cursor and Gemini CLI.
aib_coros_own_2: Since 21 September 2026 it creates workouts and 4 to 16-week plans for road running, trail running and cycling. Deleting them is done in the COROS app.
aib_coros_own_3: It reads COROS data only: workouts, daily health, HRV, sleep, EvoLab load and fitness.
aib_coros_oa_write: Plans running, trail and cycling sessions in your calendar, with targets from your zones; they go to your COROS.
aib_coros_vs_note: If COROS is your only device and you train alone, COROS's own MCP may be all you need. OpenAthlete earns its place with one calendar for load and form, other devices, a coach, or your data on your own server.
aib_coros_faq_1_q: Is there an official COROS MCP server?
aib_coros_faq_1_a: Yes. COROS runs one at mcp.coros.com/mcp, and since September 2026 it can create workouts and plans as well as read your data. OpenAthlete itself connects to your COROS account through that server.
aib_coros_faq_2_a: For what COROS's server doesn't hold: training load and form across all your devices, a calendar your coach sees too, periods for illness or travel, workouts with targets from your zones, and up to 60 sessions in one request. It is also open source and can run on your own server.
aib_coros_faq_3_q: Which workouts reach the COROS watch?
aib_coros_faq_3_a: Running, trail running and cycling. Other sports stay in the OpenAthlete calendar. COROS does not let apps delete a planned session, so if the assistant deletes one, COROS keeps a placeholder marked as removed.
aib_coros_faq_4_a: It is new (November 2026). History arrives over several days because COROS serves 50 activity files a day. If something looks off, tell us on GitHub or Discord.
aib_suunto_seo_title: Suunto + Claude/ChatGPT: your Suunto data in AI, via MCP
aib_suunto_seo_description: Connect Suunto to Claude or ChatGPT with OpenAthlete's MCP server: ask about activities, sleep, HRV and load, and send planned workouts to your watch.
aib_suunto_h1: Your Suunto training, in Claude and ChatGPT
aib_suunto_lead: OpenAthlete syncs your Suunto activities, sleep and HRV through Suunto's official API. Connect it to Claude or ChatGPT, ask about your training, and have the assistant plan sessions that reach your watch as Suunto guides.
aib_suunto_chat_prompt: Saturday is 3 × 15' at marathon pace. Do my last two long runs say I'm ready, or should I trim it?
aib_suunto_chat_reply: Your 28 and 30 km long runs held 5:05/km with heart rate in zone 2 until km 24, and you noted “legs fine” after both. Saturday looks right. I'd only take 5' easy between blocks instead of 3'. Shall I update it? It will reach your Race S as a guide.
aib_suunto_auth_contrast: The community Suunto MCP servers we looked at have you register your own app on Suunto's developer portal and wait weeks for approval. OpenAthlete already has access to Suunto's API: you sign in with Suunto and OpenAthlete receives a token.
aib_suunto_activities: Every new activity, with laps, as soon as Suunto notifies OpenAthlete
aib_suunto_metrics: Sleep stages and score, HRV, daily heart rate, SpO2, steps, calories, naps, body resources
aib_suunto_watch: Yes, as Suunto guides: running, trail running, cycling, swimming and more
aib_suunto_p1: Sleep score under 60 three nights this week. Show me the trend and move my intervals if needed.
aib_suunto_p2: Plan an 8-week build to a sub-3 marathon from my current records. Long runs on Sundays, intervals on Tuesdays, on my Suunto.
aib_suunto_p3: How has my weekly running volume compared with my cycling since August?
aib_suunto_p4: I'm in Chamonix next week with only my running shoes. Turn the bike sessions into runs.
aib_suunto_p5: Which of my last ten runs were planned sessions I actually hit, and which did I cut short?
aib_suunto_own_1: Suunto AI Coach, in the Suunto app since 15 October 2026: conversation over your Suunto data, structured workouts and routes. It launched with the Race 3S (three months included) and reaches more watches in early 2027.
aib_suunto_own_2: Suunto's Chinese site documents a read-only MCP server (mcp.suunto.cn). We found no equivalent documented for the global Suunto app.
aib_suunto_own_3: Community MCP servers exist; they need your own app on Suunto's developer portal.
aib_suunto_oa_write: Plans sessions in your calendar; they reach your watch as Suunto guides.
aib_suunto_vs_note: Suunto AI Coach lives in the Suunto app. OpenAthlete is for when you want Claude or ChatGPT, other devices in the same history, or a calendar shared with a coach.
aib_suunto_faq_1_q: Does Suunto have an MCP server?
aib_suunto_faq_1_a: Suunto's Chinese site documents a read-only one (mcp.suunto.cn). We found none documented for the global Suunto app on 3 November 2026. Suunto's own assistant, Suunto AI Coach, lives inside the Suunto app.
aib_suunto_faq_2_q: Can ChatGPT send a workout to my Suunto watch?
aib_suunto_faq_2_a: Through OpenAthlete, yes. The assistant plans the session in your OpenAthlete calendar. With workout export on, it is sent to Suunto as a guide and shows up on the watch once the Suunto app has synced.
aib_suunto_faq_3_q: Is this the same as Suunto AI Coach?
aib_suunto_faq_3_a: No. Suunto AI Coach is Suunto's assistant inside the Suunto app. OpenAthlete lets the assistant you already use, Claude or ChatGPT, work on your Suunto data alongside other devices and a coach. You can use both.
aib_suunto_faq_4_q: How much Suunto history will the AI see?
aib_suunto_faq_4_a: The last 30 days when you connect, then every new activity. Upload older FIT files to fill the gap.
aib_polar_seo_title: Polar + Claude/ChatGPT: your Polar data in AI, via MCP
aib_polar_seo_description: Connect Polar to Claude or ChatGPT through OpenAthlete's MCP server: activities, sleep and nightly HRV. Plans go to your calendar, not to the watch.
aib_polar_h1: Ask Claude or ChatGPT about your Polar training
aib_polar_lead: OpenAthlete syncs your Polar activities, sleep and nightly HRV through Polar's official AccessLink API, and Claude or ChatGPT read them over MCP. The assistant can plan your weeks in the OpenAthlete calendar, but those sessions stay there: Polar's API doesn't accept workouts, so nothing is sent to your watch.
aib_polar_chat_prompt: My nightly HRV dropped after Tuesday's intervals and hasn't come back. What should I change this week?
aib_polar_chat_reply: Your HRV was around 62 ms before Tuesday and has sat near 51 since, with resting HR up 3 bpm. Tuesday was also your hardest session in a month. I'd make Thursday an easy 40' and push Saturday's tempo to Sunday. I can change both in your OpenAthlete calendar; Polar doesn't take planned workouts, so you'll follow them from there.
aib_polar_auth_contrast: Polar's AccessLink uses OAuth: you sign in on Polar's page and OpenAthlete receives a token, never your password. Community Polar MCP servers read the same API, so they can't send workouts to the watch either.
aib_polar_activities: Every new activity, with the recording, through Polar's notifications and an hourly check
aib_polar_history: None: Polar only shares activities recorded after you connect. Upload older files to add them
aib_polar_metrics: Sleep, nightly HRV, resting and max heart rate, VO2max, weight, daily activity
aib_polar_watch: No: Polar's API doesn't accept workouts. Follow plans in OpenAthlete, on your phone, or in Google or Apple Calendar through the iCal feed
aib_polar_p1: Show my nightly HRV and sleep for the last six weeks next to my weekly load. Do they move together?
aib_polar_p2: Plan four weeks of base training in my calendar: five hours a week, mostly zone 2, one tempo session.
aib_polar_p3: Compare this spring's 10 km race with last weekend's. Same course: how did heart rate and pace differ?
aib_polar_p4: I've got the flu. Clear the next five days and rebuild the following week gently.
aib_polar_p5: What is my best 5 km this year, and what does it say about a realistic 10 km goal?
aib_polar_own_1: No MCP server or AI chat assistant from Polar that we could find.
aib_polar_own_2: Polar's AccessLink API shares exercises, daily activity, sleep, Nightly Recharge and cardio load, but offers no way to send workouts to a watch.
aib_polar_own_3: Community MCP servers read that same API, so they are read-only too.
aib_polar_oa_write: Plans sessions in your OpenAthlete calendar only. They can't be sent to Polar; the iCal feed puts them in your phone's calendar.
aib_polar_vs_note: With Polar, the calendar does the work: the assistant plans, you see the session in OpenAthlete or your phone's calendar, and Polar records what you did.
aib_polar_faq_1_q: Does Polar have an MCP server?
aib_polar_faq_1_a: We found no official one on 3 November 2026. Community servers read Polar's AccessLink API. OpenAthlete reads the same API and adds a calendar, training load and the tools to plan.
aib_polar_faq_2_q: Can Claude send a workout to my Polar watch?
aib_polar_faq_2_a: No. Polar's API has no way for apps to send workouts, so no third-party tool can. The assistant plans the session in your OpenAthlete calendar, and you follow it from the app, your phone, or Google or Apple Calendar through the iCal feed.
aib_polar_faq_3_q: Will the AI see my old Polar sessions?
aib_polar_faq_3_a: Not automatically: Polar only shares activities recorded after you connect. Export older sessions from Polar Flow as TCX or GPX files and drop them on the OpenAthlete calendar.
aib_polar_faq_4_q: Does the AI see my sleep and HRV?
aib_polar_faq_4_a: Yes, once you turn on metric import for Polar in OpenAthlete (it is off by default). Sleep, nightly HRV, resting heart rate and VO2max then come in each day, and the assistant reads them with get_metrics.

tools_links_gap_app: Grade-adjusted pace on every activity you sync
tools_trail_card: A finish-time window from distance, D+ and a race you have already run.
tools_trail_seo_description: Estimate your trail race time from distance and elevation with km-effort: a time window, pace per km-effort and average speed, from a recent race.
tools_trail_h1: Trail race time estimator with km-effort
tools_trail_lead: Enter the race distance and elevation, then a race you have already run. You get a finish-time window, the pace per km-effort and the average speed, with the formula under the result.
tools_trail_optional: D− is optional: leave it empty on a loop. It adds the course profile to the result.
tools_trail_window_note: Low end with a Riegel exponent of {low}, high end with {high}.
tools_trail_profile: On average {up} m up and {down} m down per km
tools_trail_descent_note: This course loses more height than it gains. Km-effort gives descents neither credit nor penalty: on long, steep ones, your quads set the pace, not your lungs.
tools_trail_road_note: From a road race, the estimate assumes runnable trails and carries your road speed onto the climbs. On technical ground, expect to finish past the window.
tools_trail_how_body: Km-effort turns climbing into distance: km-effort = km + D+ / 100, so every 100 m of ascent counts as one extra kilometre. Your reference race gives a time over its own km-effort. The estimate scales it with Riegel's formula applied to km-effort: T = T_ref × (E / E_ref)^k. The exponent k is set to 1.06, Riegel's road value, for the low end, and to 1.10 for the high end, to allow for the extra slowdown of long days on trails. Both are assumptions, not measurements, which is why you get a window rather than a time to the minute.
tools_trail_how_example: Example: a 25 km race with 1,000 m D+ is 35 km-effort. Finished in 3:00:00, that is 5:09 per km-effort. For a 42 km race with 2,000 m D+ (62 km-effort): 3:00:00 × (62 / 35)^1.06 = 5h30, and 3:00:00 × (62 / 35)^1.10 = 5h38. So 5h30 to 5h38, about 5:20 per km-effort and 7.5 km/h.
tools_trail_how_variants: Variants: 100 m of climbing per kilometre is the usual French convention. Some coaches weight climbing differently on very steep or very runnable courses, and some add part of the descent. ITRA uses the same sum, distance + D+ / 100, to classify races. This calculator is not affiliated with ITRA and does not compute an ITRA or UTMB index.
tools_trail_how_source: Sources: km-effort is a French trail running convention, also used by ITRA to classify races. The exponent comes from Peter Riegel, "Athletic Records and Human Endurance", American Scientist, vol. 69, 1981. The 1.10 upper bound is our assumption for long trail races, not a published value.
tools_trail_limits_title: What the formula does not know
tools_trail_limit_terrain: Terrain. Rocks, roots, mud, snow and scree slow you more than the elevation says. Two races with the same km-effort can finish far apart.
tools_trail_limit_night: Night. A head torch narrows what you see, and technical descents go slower in the dark.
tools_trail_limit_altitude: Altitude. Above about 2,000 m, the same effort gives a slower pace, more so if you live low.
tools_trail_limit_heat: Heat. A valley at 2 pm in July costs time, and the formula does not read the forecast.
tools_trail_limit_aid: Aid stations. A trail reference already includes the stops you made; a longer race means more of them, and longer. A road reference includes none.
tools_trail_faq1_a: A distance that counts the climbing: kilometres plus one per 100 m of ascent. A 30 km race with 1,500 m D+ is 45 km-effort. It lets you compare a mountain 30 km with a flat 45 km, and it is how French trail runners talk about how hard a race is.
tools_trail_faq2_q: Why a time window and not a single time?
tools_trail_faq2_a: Because the slowdown over long trail races varies a lot from one runner to the next. The window goes from a Riegel exponent of 1.06, the classic road value, to 1.10, for a runner who fades more on long days. If your long races usually go to plan, aim for the low end.
tools_trail_faq3_q: Should I enter a trail race or a road race?
tools_trail_faq3_a: A trail race, if you have one: it already contains your climbing, your descending and your stops. From a road race, the estimate assumes runnable trails and is often optimistic on technical courses. The closer the reference is to the target in km-effort and terrain, the better.
tools_trail_faq4_q: Does it work for an ultra?
tools_trail_faq4_a: It gives an order of magnitude. Past roughly 100 km-effort, sleep, food, night sections and time at aid stations weigh more than any formula. Take the high end of the window as a starting point, then check it against the cut-offs and the results of runners you know.
tools_trail_faq5_q: Is this my ITRA performance index?
tools_trail_faq5_a: No. ITRA uses km-effort to classify races, but its performance index compares your results with other runners' in its database. This page only scales one of your own results. It is not affiliated with ITRA or UTMB.
tools_gap_card: Hill pace to flat pace and back, from −20% to +30%.
tools_gap_seo_description: Grade-adjusted pace calculator: flat-equivalent pace on any slope, or the pace to hold on a climb, from Minetti's 2002 formula, with a −20% to +30% table.
tools_gap_lead: Turn a pace on a hill into its flat equivalent, or find the pace to hold on a climb for a given effort. Same model as the grade-adjusted pace OpenAthlete computes on your runs.
tools_gap_mode: What do you want to know?
tools_gap_mode_to_flat: Flat equivalent of a hill pace
tools_gap_mode_to_slope: Pace to hold on a slope
tools_gap_pace_flat: The effort, as a flat pace
tools_gap_grade_hint: Negative for a descent. Capped at ±30%, as in the app.
tools_gap_result_slope: Pace to hold on this slope
tools_gap_cost: Each metre costs {ratio} × a flat metre.
tools_gap_table_title: Same effort as {pace}/km on the flat
tools_gap_downhill_note: On steep descents the model gives the pace your heart could afford, not the one your quads, the ground and your brakes will allow.
tools_gap_how_body: Grade-adjusted pace answers one question: what would this effort be worth on flat ground? It uses the energy cost of running on a slope, measured by Minetti and colleagues on a treadmill between −45% and +45%: C(i) = 155.4i⁵ − 30.4i⁴ − 43.3i³ + 46.3i² + 19.5i + 3.6, in joules per kilogram per metre, where i is the gradient as a fraction (0.10 for 10%). On the flat, C = 3.6. Flat-equivalent pace = pace on the slope × 3.6 / C(i). The other way round, the pace to hold on a slope = flat pace × C(i) / 3.6.
tools_gap_how_example: Example: 6:00/km on a 10% climb. C(0.10) = 5.97, 1.66 times the flat cost, so 6:00/km uphill is worth 3:37/km on the flat. The other way: to keep a 5:00/km flat effort on that climb, hold 8:17/km.
tools_gap_how_app: OpenAthlete applies the same curve to every run and trail run you sync: the gradient is read from altitude over 10 m windows and capped at ±30%, because steeper readings are usually GPS or barometer noise.
tools_gap_how_source: Source: Minetti A.E., Moia C., Roi G.S., Susta D., Ferretti G., "Energy cost of walking and running at extreme uphill and downhill slopes", Journal of Applied Physiology 93, 2002 (doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.01177.2001).
tools_gap_faq1_a: The pace you would have run on flat ground for the same energy. 7:00/km on a 12% climb is worth about 3:52/km on the flat, a harder effort than 4:30/km on the road. GAP puts both on the same scale, so you can compare a hilly run with a flat one, or check you held the right effort on a climb.
tools_gap_faq2_q: Why does Strava show a different GAP?
tools_gap_faq2_a: Strava uses its own model, which it says it built from its athletes' heart rate data rather than from lab measurements of energy cost. It gives less credit on descents than Minetti's curve. Neither is wrong; they answer slightly different questions. OpenAthlete uses Minetti, written out in its open-source code, and so does this page.
tools_gap_faq3_a: On paper, yes. The curve bottoms out around −20%, where a metre costs half as much as on the flat, then rises again on steeper ground. In practice, past about −10%, braking, footing and the load on your quads limit speed before energy does. That is why a 4:30/km descent at −10% shows a flat equivalent of 7:32/km: easy for the heart, not always for the legs.
tools_gap_faq4_q: What if I hike the climbs?
tools_gap_faq4_a: The curve is for running. Minetti's team measured walking too, and on steep climbs walking costs less than running at the same speed, which is why everyone starts hiking past a certain gradient. On a power-hiked climb, read the flat-equivalent pace as a rough guide.
tools_gap_faq5_q: Can I use it for a treadmill incline?
tools_gap_faq5_a: Yes: type the incline as the gradient. 5:00/km at 5% is worth about 3:51/km on the flat. Minetti's measurements were made on a treadmill, so there is no air resistance in them; many runners set 1% to make up for its absence on a flat treadmill run (Jones and Doust, 1996).

pacechart_eq_body: Peter Riegel's formula (T2 = T1 × (D2 / D1)^1.06) turns one race time into another. Read it the other way round: if your latest {bench} is well slower than {benchTime}, the goal is ambitious for this season.
pacechart_eq_note: The marathon side of these figures assumes marathon-specific training: long runs past 30 km and enough weekly volume. Without it, most runners finish slower than Riegel predicts.

pacechart_tp_body: Jack Daniels sums up a performance in one number, VDOT. This goal works out at VDOT {vdot}, and his tables derive five intensities from it. They are the paces of the runner you are training to become: if your races are slower today, train at today's paces and move them as you improve.
pacechart_tp_easy_desc: Most of the week. You can hold a conversation.
pacechart_tp_threshold_desc: Comfortably hard: 20 minutes in one go, or 5 × 6' with short rests.
pacechart_tp_interval_desc: Reps of 3 to 5 minutes, close to VO2max.
pacechart_tp_repetition_desc: Short and fast, 200 to 400 m, full recovery.

If the third block feels controlled, the goal holds. If you have to fight for the pace from the second one, adjust the goal now rather than at kilometre 30.

pacechart_faq1_a: {pace} per kilometre, which is {mile} per mile or {speed} km/h. Held evenly, it brings you home in {time}. Courses are measured on the shortest line, so your watch will probably read a few hundred metres more: aim a couple of seconds per kilometre faster than the chart.
pacechart_marathon_faq2_q: What half marathon time do I need for a {time} marathon?
pacechart_marathon_faq2_a: About {half} for the half marathon, or {tenk} for the 10K, by Riegel's formula. Treat these as minimums: they assume marathon-specific training, with long runs past 30 km. Runners who race shorter distances well but skip the long runs usually finish the marathon several minutes slower.
pacechart_half_faq2_q: What 10K time do I need for a {time} half marathon?
pacechart_half_faq2_a: About {tenk} for the 10K, or {fivek} for the 5K, by Riegel's formula. Over the half marathon the prediction is usually close, as long as your weekly volume lets you hold a hard effort for twice as long.
pacechart_faq3_q: Should I run even pace or a negative split?
pacechart_faq3_a: Either works as long as the gap stays small. Even pace puts you through halfway in {halfway}. The negative-split version passes in {first} and runs the second half in {second}. Starting faster than the chart rarely pays: the seconds banked early come back, with interest, at the end.

trailplan_schedule_lead: Every session with its target. Sessions marked “structured” carry step-by-step targets for your watch: a share of your VMA on flat ground, a share of your max heart rate on climbs, effort (RPE 1–10) on descents.
trailplan_targets_title: Targets that become your own numbers
trailplan_targets_body: The plan never gives a pace in minutes per kilometre, because it does not know you. Flat and rolling sessions are written as a share of your VMA; climbs as a share of your max heart rate, because pace on a 12% slope tells you nothing; descents as effort. Once you import the plan, OpenAthlete reads the VMA and max heart rate in your profile and sends each structured session to your Garmin, COROS or Suunto with your own paces and heart rates.

trailplan_coach_1_body: Uphill reps of 1' to 2'30 at 88–95% of max heart rate, jogging back down. They build the strength to keep running where others start walking.
trailplan_coach_2_body: 5 to 12 minutes of steady climbing at 82–87% of max heart rate: the effort you will hold on the long climbs of the race, rehearsed.
trailplan_coach_3_body: Above 15%, most runners walk on race day. Walking fast with poles is a skill: short steps, hands pushing down, then running again as soon as the slope eases.
trailplan_coach_4_body: Short reps on a technical descent at controlled effort. Quick steps, eyes a few metres ahead, arms out. Descents are where quads give up and where time is lost.
trailplan_coach_5_title: Long runs in time and D+
trailplan_coach_5_body: Long runs grow in duration and climbing together, with a lighter week every 3–4 weeks. In the 50 km plan, weekends become back-to-back long runs to train tired legs.
trailplan_coach_6_body: Optional, 30 minutes at home: step-ups, slow single-leg squats, calf raises, balance on one leg. Then a 2-week taper so you start fresh.

From 5K to 10K the prediction is usually close for runners who train four times a week or more. With less volume, the time goes in the second half of the 10K: expect to finish a little slower than the formula says.
pacechart_5k_faq2_a: About {tenk} for the 10K and {half} for the half marathon, by Riegel's formula. Read it with care: the 5K leans on speed, longer races on endurance. Runners who train short and fast often race the 5K well and the half slower than predicted; marathoners dropping down to the 5K usually show the opposite.
pacechart_10k_wo_body: Half the race at goal pace, cut into pieces. Run it three to two weeks before race day. If the fifth kilometre is your fastest and a sixth would go, {time} is within reach. If the jog feels too short from the third rep, start the race on a slower goal and finish strong. Once it feels easy, move on to 3 × 2 km with a 400 m jog.
pacechart_5k_wo_body: Almost the whole race at goal pace, with breaks. Run it three to two weeks before race day. If the last two reps are no slower than the first, {time} holds. If you are fighting from the third, take the next chart down. For the final fortnight, a sharper version: 10 × 400 m slightly faster than goal pace, with a 200 m jog.
pacechart_short_splits_body: The even column holds {pace}/km from the gun. The negative-split column runs the first half 1% slower ({slow}/km) and the second half 1% faster ({fast}/km): {first} at halfway, then {second} for the rest. Over this distance the classic mistake is the first kilometre: fresh legs, a crowd going off fast, and you pass the marker ten seconds up without noticing. Those seconds come back with interest in the second half. Go through 1 km no faster than {km1}.

races_trail_principles_title: Four things no long trail forgives you for skipping
races_trail_p1_b: Four to six weekends before the taper, run long on Saturday and again on Sunday on tired legs: 4 h then 3 h, on terrain like the race. It teaches the legs and the stomach to keep going without one 8-hour run that wrecks a week.
races_trail_p2_b: Run with your race headlamp at least three or four times, on trails, after dark. Footing is slower, sleepiness hits around 3 am, and you want to know your battery life before the race tells you.
races_trail_p3_b: On long climbs, most runners walk. Train it: 20 to 40 min of steep uphill hiking with poles, once a week. If poles are allowed and you plan to use them, never race with them for the first time.
races_trail_p4_b: Quads fail on the way down, not up. Run long downhills every week from three months out, add step-downs and lunges, and practise technical ground at an easy pace until it feels boring.
races_trail_cta_body: Build the block in OpenAthlete: plan the back-to-back weekends in the calendar, write the hill sessions once, and send them to your Garmin, COROS or Suunto watch.

races_faq_when_road_a: Our marathon plans last 16 weeks, so start on {date}. You need a base first: running three or four times a week for a few months, with a long run of about 1h15 already comfortable.

races_paris_meta: Paris Marathon on 4 April 2027: pace for every goal, the Monday to start a free 16-week plan, and how to handle the hills in the woods.
races_paris_lead: Sunday 4 April 2027, the 50th edition. The 2027 course comes out only a few weeks before the race, so train for what Paris usually throws at you: rolling woods, tunnels on the quays and a hard last 8 km.
races_paris_period: 50th edition. First entry by lottery; the official bib resale opens on 1 December 2026.

races_paris_course: City course on asphalt. The press expects the start to stay on the Champs-Élysées; the organisers will reveal the 2027 route a few weeks before race day.
races_paris_weather: Early April: 8 to 17 °C on average (Météo-France normals, Paris-Montsouris). Cool mornings.
races_paris_hub: Rolling woods, quay tunnels and a 2027 course still under wraps.
races_paris_s1_t: Not as flat as it looks
races_paris_s1_b: On the 2026 course the climbing sat in the two woods: short ups and downs in the Bois de Vincennes from km 10 to 20, and a long false flat in the Bois de Boulogne from km 37. Expect something similar. Run one long run in three on rolling roads and hold the effort, not the pace, on every rise.
races_paris_s2_b: A 16-week plan starts on Monday 14 December 2026, so Christmas and New Year land in weeks 2 and 3. Good: those are easy weeks anyway. The real work falls in January and February, in the dark and the cold. Book your long runs in daylight at the weekend and keep the treadmill for the intervals.
races_paris_s3_t: Save something for the last 8 km
races_paris_s3_b: In 2026 the quays brought two tunnels that break your rhythm, then a steep 500 m climb around km 33 and the Boulogne false flat. Finish your goal-pace long runs with 5 km on a slight uphill, and on race day let the tunnel descents roll without chasing the time lost on the way up.
races_paris_faq1_a: Sunday 4 April 2027, for the 50th edition. Bibs went by lottery for the first time (applications closed on 30 September 2026). The organisers also list charity bibs, corporate packages, tour operators and an official resale platform opening on 1 December 2026.
races_paris_faq2_a: Mostly, but not completely. A press analysis of the 2026 course counted about 290 m of climbing, spread over the Bois de Vincennes, the tunnels on the quays and the Bois de Boulogne. The 2027 course is not published yet: check the official site in early 2027.
